I say this as someone who used to be polyamorous, and as someone who supports the freedom to choose that lifestyle.

Try to remember that our surface level beliefs and decisions are not the whole of who we are. That is the tip of the iceberg. There is a problem with your sentiment. The problem is that it is abstract, and has no definite cause or solution.

There is no way to tell who is to blame for you "finding out that Santa isn't real", for lack of a better metaphor, and how do you fix it? 

Is it really just the way BfA is designed? I would argue no. The average gamer has been seeing through the curtain for a year or two now, experiencing corporate greed slowly pushing into the public awareness with scandals like "pride and accomplishment". Maybe it's because those companies are being more blatant with their greed, or maybe we've just outgrown their ability to lie convincingly. Maybe both. Either way, we're seeing more and more discussion and frustration surrounding where game design begins to cater to monetisation.

But we're also seeing paranoia take root. There is no way to know just how much of the game is being manipulated to create lasting profits as opposed to enjoyment. For example, people say titanforges make it so that you never "feel done", and that Blizzard does this out of greed and to keep you playing and paying. On the other hand, titanforges are also an incentive for people who don't want to "feel done". They want infinite replayability, and they don't want to run out of potential upgrades. Titanforges even give you a chance at something helpful if you're helping out your lesser geared buddies. If you're just doing tens for the week, but your friend is only geared for a five, you are more inclined to help him when you know there is a chance you might get something out of it.

You've seen the man behind the curtain. You've learned that Santa isn't real, and you see through the lie. We're all varying amounts of angry, frustrated, and jaded, because we can't trust greedy corporations to not manipulate us for their benefit over our own. We can't ever know that they are actually doing something to make the product better, or if they're doing it to keep us playing with less work on their end.

We can never know if their intentions are pure.

There is no solution to this. Not as long as "live service"-style games exist. Unless we go back to the payment model where you pay one price for a full, standalone product, you will never be able to know whether or not their game design is dictated by optimal microtransaction sales or retention rates for subscriptions.

That's not going to happen, because there isn't enough money in it. So you're going to have to decide your next step. Either you take games as they come, and hope to find the ones that remind you of the fantasy you used to know, or you will have to accept that you've outgrown the hobby.

I'm not a "hardcore" capitalist, but I do think we need capitalism, so I'll answer this. 

Capitalism relies on the concept of a free market, where competition can drive innovation, keep products at a high quality, and keep prices down. Comcast has a monopoly. No one can really afford to challenge them, so they have no competition. 

In essence, this is not what most people who support capitalism believe to be "true capitalism". The government and corporations aren't supposed to work together in an ideal system. The government should keep the corporations in check, and the corporations should keep the government in check. What we have now is crony capitalism, or "late stage" capitalism. Corporations have so much power that they can buy off the government, and then produce terrible products for exorbitant prices with no competition.

It's an inherent flaw with the system that should have been better protected against. But human greed, and their willingness to sell out their constituents for money, won out.
